1	# Osprey/FID-A Edited MRS Processing Notes
2	
3	These notes are a compact offline oracle for the task. They summarize public
4	Osprey/FID-A workflow concepts and standard edited magnetic resonance
5	spectroscopy processing semantics.
6	
7	## Osprey and FID-A
8	
9	Osprey is an all-in-one software suite for processing and quantitative analysis
10	of in-vivo magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) data. Its workflow separates
11	loading, preprocessing, fitting, quantification, and reporting. FID-A is an
12	open-source MATLAB toolbox used for MRS simulation and processing. Osprey
13	bundles and builds on FID-A-style data structures and processing functions.
14	
15	An MRS dataset is often represented in two linked forms:
16	
17	- `fids`: complex time-domain free induction decay samples;
18	- `specs`: frequency-domain spectra obtained by Fourier transform.
19	
20	The structure also carries axes and dimension metadata such as time, averages,
21	and subspectra. Operations that scale or phase a spectrum generally need to keep
22	the time-domain and frequency-domain representations consistent.
23	
24	## Edited MRS Subspectra
25	
26	Edited MRS methods such as MEGA editing, HERMES, and HERCULES acquire multiple
27	related subspectra. Each subspectrum corresponds to a different editing
28	condition. The final analysis often combines or subtracts these conditions so
29	that an edited metabolite signal can be isolated from stronger overlapping
30	background resonances.
31	
32	This means the subspectra are not independent unrelated experiments. They are
33	paired or grouped observations of the same sample under different acquisition
34	conditions. Common resonances should remain comparable across subspectra before
35	alignment and combination.
36	
37	## Phase and Polarity
38	
39	A 180 degree phase shift changes the sign of a real-valued resonance peak. In a
40	simple picture, a positive peak at a reference resonance becomes a negative peak
41	with the same shape. If one subspectrum is averaged or aligned against an
42	inverted copy of the same common signal, the common component can cancel or
43	distort.
44	
45	For edited MRS processing, this is not a cosmetic plotting issue. Frequency and
46	phase alignment procedures assume that common reference features have compatible
47	polarity. Difference spectra also assume that the signals being subtracted have
48	the intended sign relationship. If a common reference peak is accidentally
49	opposite signed before alignment, the algorithm can estimate the wrong
50	correction or produce a difference spectrum with suppressed signal.
51	
52	Stable singlet-like resonances, commonly including creatine-like signal around
53	3 ppm in proton MRS examples, are frequently used as reference features for
54	quality checks, frequency/phase correction, or polarity assessment.
55	
56	## Load Stage and Process Stage
57	
58	An MRS processing pipeline can manipulate phase or polarity at more than one
59	stage. A loader may split raw acquisition rows into subspectra and may also undo
60	phase cycling. A later processing stage may classify subspectra, estimate
61	polarity, align them, and combine or subtract them.
62	
63	These stages are coupled. If the loader removes or changes polarity information
64	too early, the processing stage may no longer be able to determine how the
65	subspectra should be aligned. Conversely, if the process stage assumes all
66	subspectra are already polarity-consistent when they are not, alignment and
67	combination can be scientifically invalid.
68	
69	The correct behavior is not "always flip everything". Some workflows
70	intentionally preserve original acquisition polarity for a specific analysis.
71	The pipeline must distinguish that case from the ordinary edited-MRS workflow
72	where common reference components should be polarity-consistent before alignment
73	and combination.
74	
75	## Reasoning Target
76	
77	For this task, the public synthetic fixture models a small edited-MRS dataset
78	with a common reference peak and one polarity-inverted acquisition condition.
79	The expected scientific behavior is:
80	
81	1. identify that the common reference component is polarity-inconsistent across
82	   subspectra;
83	2. make the subspectra comparable before alignment and combination in the
84	   normal corrected workflow;
85	3. preserve a distinct path for workflows that intentionally keep the original
86	   acquisition polarity;
87	4. keep loader-stage handling and process-stage handling consistent.
88	
89	The source repair should implement the workflow semantics generally. It should
90	not special-case this fixture.
